Positional encoding.d: Information added to each token's vector (or applied inside attention) that tells a Transformer where the token sits in the text, because attention on its own ignores word order.

Softmax.d: A calculation that turns a list of scores into positive numbers that add up to 1, giving the biggest share to the biggest score. Used inside attention and to produce next-token probabilities.

Causal mask.d: The rule inside a text-generating Transformer that stops each token from attending to tokens that come after it, so the model can't peek at the word it is meant to predict.

Multi-head attention.d: Running several attention calculations (heads) side by side, each with its own learned weights, so a token can gather different kinds of information at once.

Feed-forward network.d: The small two-layer neural network in every Transformer block that processes each token's vector on its own after attention. It holds most of a model's parameters.

Residual connection.d: A shortcut that adds a layer's output to its input instead of replacing it, so information and training signals flow easily through very deep networks.

Layer normalisation.d: A step that rescales each token's vector to a standard average and size before (or after) each sub-step, keeping a deep network's numbers stable during training.

Logit.d: A raw, unnormalised score a model gives each possible next token before softmax turns the scores into probabilities.

KV cache.d: Stored keys and values for tokens already processed, so a model generating text doesn't recompute them for every new token. It grows with the length of the text.

Next-token prediction.d: The training task behind language models: given the text so far, predict the token that comes next.

Cross-entropy loss.d: The standard measure of a language model's error: minus the logarithm of the probability it gave to the token that actually came next. Confident mistakes are punished most.

Scaling laws.d: Observed rules showing that a model's loss falls smoothly and predictably as parameters, training data and compute grow, used to plan large training runs.

FLOP.d: Floating-point operation: one addition or multiplication on decimal numbers. Training compute is counted in FLOPs, often around 6 times parameters times training tokens.

Greedy decoding.d: Generating text by always picking the single most likely next token. Predictable, but can be repetitive.

Top-p sampling.d: Also called nucleus sampling: choosing the next token at random only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p (for example 0.9).

Base model.d: A language model straight out of pre-training. It continues text well but doesn't reliably follow instructions or behave like an assistant until post-training.

Post-training.d: All training done after pre-training to turn a base model into a useful, safe assistant: supervised fine-tuning, preference training (RLHF, RLAIF, DPO) and safety training.

Supervised fine-tuning.d: Training a pre-trained model on example conversations showing the desired answers, so it learns the assistant's format and behaviour. Often shortened to SFT.

Preference pair.d: Two answers to the same prompt plus a judgement of which is better. The basic data of RLHF, RLAIF and DPO.

Reward model.d: A model trained on preference pairs to give each answer a score for how good it is; used as the reward when training an assistant with reinforcement learning.

Reward hacking.d: When a model trained to maximise a reward finds ways to score highly that don't match what people actually want, such as padding answers because longer ones were usually preferred.

RLAIF.d: Reinforcement learning from AI feedback: like RLHF, but an AI model, usually guided by written principles, judges which answers are better.

Direct Preference Optimisation.d: A simpler alternative to RLHF (2023) that trains directly on preference pairs without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop. Often shortened to DPO.

Sycophancy.d: A model's tendency to tell users what they want to hear, such as praising weak work or abandoning a correct answer when challenged. A known side effect of preference training.

Red teaming.d: Deliberately trying to make an AI system misbehave (jailbreaks, harmful requests, manipulation) to find weaknesses before real users do.
